beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string only from a runtime-secret store or environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never commit it to source control, logs, or test fixtures.
Use a dedicated least-privilege database user/account for the application (create a DB user with only the required roles for the sample database) rather than the cluster admin/root credentials.
Always enable TLS/SSL for connections to the cluster and validate server certificates; do not disable certificate checking in production code.

Configure the MongoDB driver connection pool (e.g., maxPoolSize) and reasonable connection/operation timeouts rather than leaving defaults to avoid resource exhaustion in long-running agent processes.
Avoid open-ended queries that return large result sets; push filtering and aggregation into server-side aggregation pipelines to reduce data transfer and memory usage on the client.

Create explicit indexes for the exact fields used by the care-gap aggregation and any common filter/sort patterns (e.g., patient_id, date_of_birth, diagnosis_codes, visit_date, last_visit_date) and prefer compound indexes matching query shapes.
For time-series-like data such as visits, consider a TTL index on fields used to drop or archive very old events, but only if automatic expiry is acceptable for your retention policy.

Model patient and visit data with embeddings where visits are separate documents referencing patient_id (normalized) when visits are many and queried independently; embed small, rarely-changing metadata inside the patient document when it simplifies queries.

When performing multi-document updates that must be atomic across collections (e.g., updating patient and visit together), use transactions if available and required for correctness; otherwise design for eventual consistency and idempotent operations.

Implement retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter for transient network errors, rate-limited responses or primary-stepdown errors, and make writes idempotent when possible (use retryable writes or idempotency keys).
Use server-side projection to return only the fields required by the agent (e.g., patient identifiers, relevant dates, risk flags) to minimize bandwidth and memory overhead.

Avoid use of $where, JavaScript execution, or unindexed regexes in queries used by the pipeline; prefer indexed operators and aggregation pipeline stages for performance and to avoid full collection scans.

When using vector search, store normalized embeddings of a fixed dimension, create the appropriate vector index (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) configured for the expected recall/latency, and include scalar filters in the same query to restrict candidates before nearest-neighbour scoring.
Set sensible limits and use pagination (range-based or limit+sort cursors) for ranked results and outreach lists to avoid loading the entire patient population into memory at once.

Index any fields used for sort operations in the aggregation pipeline (e.g., priority score, last_visit_date) or perform ranking in the pipeline so sorting can leverage an index rather than sorting huge in-memory result sets.

During local development and testing, never point test suites to production clusters; use a separate development or test database name (e.g., sample_healthcare_11) and credential, and include a .env.example with placeholders instead of real secrets.
Seed scripts should be idempotent: detect existing collections/documents and either upsert or skip to avoid duplicating test data or corrupting a shared environment.
Restrict network access to the cluster using firewall/VNet rules and application IP allowlists; do not rely solely on credentials for security.
Monitor and instrument query performance (slow query logs, index usage stats, top operations) and add or refine indexes based on observed aggregation pipeline patterns rather than guessing up-front.

For sensitive healthcare data, ensure application-level encryption or field-level encryption for PHI fields as required by compliance; do not rely solely on transport or disk encryption if policy demands separation of keys.
